entries.topic: Federal wage floors: minimum wage real value, tipped cash wage, overtime salary threshold, other frozen dollar benchmarks

claims.text: EPI (2025 dollars, CPI-U-RS based State of Working America series): the federal minimum was worth $12.11 in 1968 ($1.60 nominal), $10.45 in 2009 when it reached $7.25, $8.91 in 2020, $7.42 in 2024 and $7.25 in 2025; 1938 $0.25 = $4.65; 1950 $8.17; 1956 $9.65; 1974 $11.02; 1979 $11.21; 1989 $7.86; 1991 $9.18; 1997 $9.65; 2006 $7.86. Book arithmetic: 2025 value is 40% below 1968 and 31% below 2009.
EPI July 2022 (June 2022 dollars): $7.25 worth less than at any point since February 1956; 1968 peak $12.12; July 2009 $9.99; down 27.4% since 2009 and 40.2% since 1968.

Tip credit entered the FLSA with the 1966 amendments at 50% of the minimum wage; in 1991 the tipped cash wage was $2.13 (50% of $4.25); 1996 amendments fixed the cash wage at $2.13 while the regular minimum rose; unchanged since.

CRS RL32088: white-collar exemption weekly salary tests: 1938 $30 (executive/administrative); 1949 $55-$75; 1963 $100-$115; 1970 $125-$140; 1975 $155-$170 (upset test $250); 2004 final rule issued 23 Apr 2004.

2019 DOL rule raised the exempt threshold from the $455/week ($23,660) level in force since 2004 to $684/week ($35,568) effective 1 Jan 2020; the 2016 rule ($913/week, $47,476) was enjoined by a Texas federal court days before it was to take effect.

2024 rule: $844/week ($43,888) from 1 July 2024, $1,128/week ($58,656) from 1 Jan 2025, triennial updates; vacated nationwide 15 Nov 2024 by Judge Sean D. Jordan (E.D. Tex.) in State of Texas / Plano Chamber of Commerce v. DOL; threshold reverted to $684/week; HCE $107,432.

24 Apr 2025: DOJ asked the Fifth Circuit to hold the overtime-rule appeals in abeyance pending DOL reconsideration; May 2026: Law360 reports DOL dropped another appeal and the Fifth Circuit dismissed it. Status as of Oct 2026: $684/week applies.

SSI asset limits $2,000 individual / $3,000 couple, reached by gradual increases 1985–1989, the only increase since enactment; 1972 limits $1,500/$2,250; indexed since 1972 they would be $9,929/$14,893 in 2023; over two-thirds of SSI beneficiaries have no savings, about 92% under $500; benefits fall $1 per $2 of earnings above $65/month and dollar for dollar above $20 of other income.

June 2026: the SSI Savings Penalty Elimination Act (Sens. Cortez Masto D-NV and Cassidy R-LA; Reps. Davis D-IL and Fitzpatrick R-PA) would raise limits to $10,000/$20,000; current limits still $2,000/$3,000.

OBBBA §70433: Form 1099-MISC/NEC threshold raised from $600 (unindexed) to $2,000 for payments after 31 Dec 2025, indexed from 2027 (base 2025); 1099-K reverts to $20,000 and 200 transactions; $600 set in 1954.

BLS 2024: 843,000 hourly paid workers at or below $7.25 (82,000 at exactly $7.25, 760,000 below), 1.0% of 80.3m hourly paid workers vs 13.4% in 1979; under-25s 43% of them; leisure and hospitality 5.6% rate, about two-thirds of the total, mostly restaurants (tipped workers can legally be paid below); part-time 55.9%.

CBO (8 July 2019), $15 by 2025: 17 million workers would get raises and possibly 10 million more; median 1.3 million jobs lost (likely range about zero to 3.7 million); 1.3 million lifted out of poverty.

HHS 2026 poverty guidelines (48 states/DC): $15,960 for one person, $21,640 for two, $27,320 for three, $33,000 for four. Book arithmetic: $7.25 x 2,080 hours = $15,080, $880 below the one-person guideline and $6,560 below two.

Roosevelt's message to Congress of 24 May 1937 called for 'a fair day's pay for a fair day's work'; FLSA signed 25 June 1938, effective 24 Oct 1938, with a 25-cent minimum and a 44-hour maximum workweek, covering industries employing about one-fifth of the labour force.

DWT on the Nov 2024 ruling: DOL took the position in 2004 that automatic indexing was beyond its authority; the 2016 rule's automatic indexing was struck down; historically DOL set low salary levels designed to exclude only obviously nonexempt employees; the $684/$107,432 levels now apply.

Book arithmetic from the DOL chart: the gaps between increases were 1981–1990 (nine years) and 1997–2007 (ten years); the freeze since 24 July 2009 (over 17 years by Oct 2026) is the longest since 1938.

CBPP (Romig, Dec 2021): Congress has never raised the amount of income SSA disregards in calculating SSI benefits since creating SSI in 1972; indexed, the $65 earned-income exclusion would have been $416/month in 2021.

entries.topic: Hours, multiple jobholding, two-earner families, childcare costs

claims.text: BLS MLR (Lalé 2015): multiple-jobholding rate (ages 16–64) peaked at about 6.8% in summer 1995, about 6.2% in Jan 1994, fell to about 5.0% by end-2013; rates rise with education (college+ ~7.8% 1994 → ~6.0% 2013); May 2004 reasons: extra money 38.1%, meet expenses or pay off debt 25.6%, enjoyment 17.6%; second jobs averaged 13.5 hours/week in 1995.

BLS 2025 (11-month averages): both spouses employed in 49.1% of married-couple families; both parents employed in 66.3% of married-couple families with children under 18; mothers' labour force participation 73.9% (children under 18), 68.0% (children under 6).
BLS: labour force participation of mothers with children under 18 was 47% in March 1975 and 73% in March 2000 (peak), 71% in 2007.

Bruenig (6 May 2019) on Warren & Tyagi: their table compared a 1970s one-earner and an early-2000s two-earner family and found less discretionary income for the latter; Bruenig argues the CPI-U deflator (vs CPI-U-RS) overstated the 1970s family's income by ~13%, category inflation was mishandled, homes were ~33% larger, and childcare ($9,600 of the higher fixed costs) is temporary; Gruber and Cullen (NBER 5608) found little evidence wives enter work when husbands lose jobs.

The Two-Income Trap (Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi, Basic Books) argued rising fixed costs (housing in good school districts, childcare, health) made middle-class families dependent on two incomes and vulnerable to bankruptcy if one is lost; reviews ranged from Madrick (main thesis undeniable) to Bruenig (bogus analysis).

2024 CCDF final rule (issued March 2024) capped family copayments for subsidised child care at 7% of family income; a new final rule published 12 May 2026, effective 13 July 2026, repealed the federal 7% cap.

MLR Fig. 2c: multiple-jobholding rate Jan 1994 vs Dec 2013 by education: less than high school 3.03% → 2.58%; high school 5.21% → 3.83%; some college 7.35% → 5.58%; college+ 7.83% → 6.00%; 'moonlighting has been trending downward within all educational groups'.

Warren and Tyagi, The Two-Income Trap (2003): two-income families earn about 75% more (inflation-adjusted) than one-earner families a generation earlier yet have less discretionary income; the main driver is a bidding war for homes in good school districts, plus health insurance, a second car, preschool; families with children nearly three times as likely to go bankrupt.

BLS Employment Situation, Sept 2026 (released 2 Oct 2026): 4.5 million employed part time for economic reasons (hours cut or unable to find full-time work), little changed. Book arithmetic: about 2.8% of roughly 163 million employed.

Delaware and Minnesota paid family and medical leave benefits scheduled from 1 Jan 2026; Maine from 1 May 2026; Maryland FAMLI postponed, contributions from 1 Jan 2027 and benefits expected from 3 Jan 2028.

entries.topic: Monopsony, noncompetes, licensing, job lock, wage theft

claims.text: Azar, Marinescu and Steinbaum: concentration computed for over 8,000 occupation-by-commuting-zone markets from CareerBuilder.com postings; the average market is highly concentrated under DOJ/FTC merger guidelines; moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of concentration is associated with a 17% decline in posted wages (panel IV).

Manning (2021) reviews mounting evidence that employers have considerable monopsony power; Caldwell, Dube and Naidu (NBER, Aug 2026) define labour market power by the firm-specific labour supply elasticity, from search frictions, preference heterogeneity and concentration, and caution markdowns and elasticities are hard to infer from one another.

Rinz (JHR 2022, Census W-2 data): local commuting-zone concentration generally declined 1976–2015 to about three-quarters of its 1976 level, while national industry concentration rose after 1990; median-to-75th-percentile move lowers earnings by nearly 10%, typical within-market change about 1%; falling local concentration left 2015 average earnings ~1% higher.

Benmelech, Bergman and Kim (Census plant data 1977–2009): local employer concentration rose over the period, is negatively related to wages, more so where unionisation is low; wage growth tracks productivity more closely in less concentrated markets.

FTC noncompete rule finalised 23 Apr 2024 (effective date set for 4 Sept 2024): about 30 million workers (roughly one in five) bound; projected $400–488bn higher earnings over ten years ($524/yr average); existing senior-executive noncompetes (>$151,164, policy-making) exempted.
Ryan LLC v. FTC (N.D. Tex., Judge Ada Brown), 20 Aug 2024: rule exceeds FTC authority and is arbitrary and capricious; set aside with nationwide effect.

5 Sept 2025: FTC voted 3–1 (Slaughter dissenting) to dismiss its appeals in Ryan (5th Cir.) and Properties of the Villages (11th Cir.) and accede to vacatur; it sought public information on noncompetes and moved toward case-by-case enforcement.

Starr, Prescott and Bishara (survey of 11,505): about 18% currently bound by a noncompete, 38% ever; found in low-wage jobs and in states where unenforceable; only 10% negotiate; about one-third receive it after accepting the offer.

2015 Treasury/CEA/DOL: less than 5% of workers covered by state licensing in the early 1950s; about 25% now (29% with local and federal); two-thirds of the rise from more professions requiring a license; 10–15% wage premium (adjusted); interstate migration ~14% lower in most-licensed occupations; prices 3–16% higher in reviewed studies. Kleiner and Krueger: 29% fully licensed, about 14% higher wages.
BLS CPS 2025 (11-month averages): 24.0% of employed had a certification or license; 21.6% a license.

West Health-Gallup (fieldwork 27 Oct–22 Dec 2025; published 21 July 2026): 24% of workers with employer coverage (about 23 million) stay in a job they want to leave for health insurance, up 8 points since 2021; 44% among those with unpayable medical debt vs 21%. Madrian (QJE 1994): job lock reduced voluntary turnover about 25% (16% to 12% a year), 1987 NMES data.

EPI (Cooper and Kroeger, 10 May 2017, CPS 2013–2015): minimum-wage violations about $8bn/yr in the 10 most populous states, 2.4 million workers (17% of low-wage eligible workers), about $3,300/yr each (23.9% of pay), extrapolated to over $15bn nationally; self-reported data, minimum-wage violations only.

EPI (20 Dec 2024): more than $1.5bn recovered 2021–2023 (DOL $659.8m for 510,534 workers; states $201.4m; top-10 2021 class settlements $641.3m); WHD investigator in 2022 responsible for almost triple the workers of a 1973 counterpart.
Broken Laws (2008 survey of 4,387 low-wage workers in Chicago, LA, NYC): 26% paid below minimum; 76% of those over 40 hours not paid overtime; 68% at least one pay violation in the previous week.

ERG for DOL (July 2014, FY2011 data): 3.5–6.8% of covered jobs in CA and NY paid below the minimum; 11–12% of low-wage jobs; over 300,000 violations a month per state; $20–29m lost per week across both states; estimates vary by data source (CPS vs SIPP).

Starr, Prescott and Bishara (abstract): noncompetes more likely in high-skill, high-paying jobs but also common in low-wage jobs and in states where unenforceable; wages tend to be lower where noncompetes are easier to enforce; early-notice noncompetes associated with better outcomes than those presented after acceptance.
